# Load the provided M0f module and run a compact demo:
# 1) Baseline vs Control (same seed) — compare headline metrics
# 2) Jitter sweep — plot MI_proxy vs jitter for model vs control (averaged across seeds)

import json
from pathlib import Path
import importlib.util
import types
import math

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

# --- Load module from /mnt/data/system_m0f.py ---
mod_path = Path("/mnt/data/system_m0f.py")
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("system_m0f", str(mod_path))
m = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
spec.loader.exec_module(m)  # type: ignore

# --- 1) Baseline vs Control ---
seed = 42
baseline = m.run_baseline(seed=seed)
control  = m.run_control(seed=seed)

cols_to_show = [
    "protocol","control","loopness","assembly_depth","repair_IoU",
    "policy_TV","policy_KL","MI_proxy","anisotropy"
]

df_bc = pd.DataFrame([{k: baseline.get(k) for k in cols_to_show},
                      {k: control.get(k)  for k in cols_to_show}])

# Reorder rows for readability
df_bc.index = ["Baseline (seed=42)", "Control (seed=42)"]

from caas_jupyter_tools import display_dataframe_to_user
display_dataframe_to_user("Baseline vs Control — headline metrics", df_bc)

# --- 2) Jitter sweep (model vs control) ---
sigmas = [0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6]
seeds  = [0, 1, 2]

records = []
for s in sigmas:
    # model
    sweep_m = m.run_jitter_sweep(sigmas=[s], seeds=seeds)
    for rec in sweep_m:
        rec2 = {**rec, "which": "model"}
        records.append(rec2)
    # control
    sweep_c = m.run_jitter_sweep(sigmas=[s], seeds=seeds, control=True)
    for rec in sweep_c:
        rec2 = {**rec, "which": "control"}
        records.append(rec2)

df = pd.DataFrame.from_records(records)

# Aggregate across seeds for plotting
agg = df.groupby(["which", "params"]).agg(
    MI_proxy_mean=("MI_proxy", "mean"),
    MI_proxy_std=("MI_proxy", "std"),
    loopness_mean=("loopness", "mean"),
    loopness_std=("loopness", "std")
).reset_index()

# Extract sigma from the nested params dict
agg["sigma"] = agg["params"].apply(lambda p: p.get("jitter"))

# Separate frames
agg_model = agg[agg["which"]=="model"].sort_values("sigma")
agg_ctrl  = agg[agg["which"]=="control"].sort_values("sigma")

# Plot MI_proxy vs jitter (one chart, no styles or explicit colors)
plt.figure()
plt.errorbar(agg_model["sigma"], agg_model["MI_proxy_mean"], yerr=agg_model["MI_proxy_std"], label="model")
plt.errorbar(agg_ctrl["sigma"],  agg_ctrl["MI_proxy_mean"],  yerr=agg_ctrl["MI_proxy_std"],  label="control")
plt.xlabel("jitter (sigma)")
plt.ylabel("MI_proxy (mean ± sd)")
plt.title("Jitter sweep: MI_proxy vs jitter (averaged over seeds)")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Also surface the aggregated table to the user
display_dataframe_to_user("Jitter sweep — aggregated metrics", agg[["which","sigma","MI_proxy_mean","MI_proxy_std","loopness_mean","loopness_std"]])

# Retry with robust fallbacks: if control variants raise, skip them and continue with model results.
import runpy
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pathlib import Path
from caas_jupyter_tools import display_dataframe_to_user

g = runpy.run_path(str(Path("/mnt/data/system_m0f.py")))
run_baseline = g["run_baseline"]
run_control = g.get("run_control")
run_jitter_sweep = g["run_jitter_sweep"]

# 1) Baseline vs Control (best-effort)
seed = 42
baseline = run_baseline(seed=seed)

cols_to_show = [
    "protocol","control","loopness","assembly_depth","repair_IoU",
    "policy_TV","policy_KL","MI_proxy","anisotropy"
]

rows = [{"label":"Baseline (seed=42)", **{k: baseline.get(k) for k in cols_to_show}}]

try:
    control  = run_control(seed=seed)
    rows.append({"label":"Control (seed=42)", **{k: control.get(k) for k in cols_to_show}})
except Exception as e:
    rows.append({"label":"Control (seed=42)", **{k: None for k in cols_to_show}})

df_bc = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("label")
display_dataframe_to_user("Baseline vs Control — headline metrics", df_bc)

# 2) Jitter sweep
sigmas = [0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6]
seeds  = [0, 1, 2]

records = []
# model
for s in sigmas:
    sweep_m = run_jitter_sweep(sigmas=[s], seeds=seeds)
    for rec in sweep_m:
        rec2 = {**rec, "which": "model"}
        records.append(rec2)

# control (best-effort)
for s in sigmas:
    try:
        sweep_c = run_jitter_sweep(sigmas=[s], seeds=seeds, control=True)
        for rec in sweep_c:
            rec2 = {**rec, "which": "control"}
            records.append(rec2)
    except Exception:
        pass

df = pd.DataFrame.from_records(records)

# Aggregate across seeds for plotting
agg = df.groupby(["which", "params"]).agg(
    MI_proxy_mean=("MI_proxy", "mean"),
    MI_proxy_std=("MI_proxy", "std"),
    loopness_mean=("loopness", "mean"),
    loopness_std=("loopness", "std")
).reset_index()

# Extract sigma from the nested params dict safely
agg["sigma"] = agg["params"].apply(lambda p: p.get("jitter") if isinstance(p, dict) else None)

# Split
agg_model = agg[agg["which"]=="model"].sort_values("sigma")
agg_ctrl  = agg[agg["which"]=="control"].sort_values("sigma")

# Plot MI_proxy vs jitter
plt.figure()
if not agg_model.empty:
    plt.errorbar(agg_model["sigma"], agg_model["MI_proxy_mean"], yerr=agg_model["MI_proxy_std"], label="model")
if not agg_ctrl.empty:
    plt.errorbar(agg_ctrl["sigma"],  agg_ctrl["MI_proxy_mean"],  yerr=agg_ctrl["MI_proxy_std"],  label="control")
plt.xlabel("jitter (sigma)")
plt.ylabel("MI_proxy (mean ± sd)")
plt.title("Jitter sweep: MI_proxy vs jitter (averaged over seeds)")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

display_dataframe_to_user("Jitter sweep — aggregated metrics", agg[["which","sigma","MI_proxy_mean","MI_proxy_std","loopness_mean","loopness_std"]])

Great question. Here’s a tight, prioritized test plan for M₀-F that hits the core behaviors and gives you plots/tables with clear comparisons—no pass/fail thresholds, just patterns and co-elevations as your HOW-TO recommends. fileciteturn0file0

# 0) Quick sanity checks (5–10 min)
- **Reproducibility:** Run the same protocol twice with the same `seed` and confirm identical metrics.
- **Seed variance:** Run baseline over ~10 seeds; visualize dispersion for `MI_proxy`, `loopness`, `assembly_depth`, `anisotropy`.
- **Runtime integrity:** Ensure each run returns a dict with the full metric set and that JSONL logging (if enabled) writes one record per line. fileciteturn0file0

# 1) Baseline vs Control (single seed, then a few seeds)
**Goal:** Establish that adding assembly + self-model changes the regime.
- **What to run:** `run_baseline(seed=S)` vs `run_control(seed=S)` for 3–5 seeds.
- **Report:** One table per seed + a summary table of means/SDs.
- **Patterns to look for:** Model tends to show higher `assembly_depth`, non-zero `policy_TV/KL` post-injection, and elevated `MI_proxy` vs control; `anisotropy` may diverge. fileciteturn0file0
- **Regression checks:** Control should not exhibit strong policy drift after the Σ nudge; flag if `policy_KL` is large.

# 2) Jitter sweep (noise sensitivity)
**Goal:** See how history-dependence and recurrence respond to input noise.
- **What to run:** `run_jitter_sweep(sigmas=[0.0,0.2,0.4,0.6], seeds=[0,1,2])` for model **and** control.
- **Report:** Plot `MI_proxy` vs jitter (mean ± SD across seeds) for model & control on the same axes; a companion plot for `loopness`.
- **Patterns to look for:** Gradual decline of `MI_proxy` and/or `loopness` with rising jitter; model curve typically above control across σ. fileciteturn0file0

> Heads-up: I hit a **shape-mismatch** while averaging step-policies in control/sweep runs (NumPy stack). Add a tiny guard in the policy aggregator (pad/trim to 6-action vectors before `np.stack`) and re-run; also add a unit test: “all policy vectors have identical shape before averaging.”

# 3) Downward causation (Σ-nudge drift)
**Goal:** Quantify how the injected self-model shifts behavior and for how long.
- **What to run:** `run_downward(seed=S)` for 3–5 seeds.
- **Report:** Bars (mean ± SD) for `policy_TV` and `policy_KL`; a line showing drift decay window if time-series is exposed.
- **Patterns to look for:** A clear mid-run increase in drift (post-injection), then decay over several hundred steps. fileciteturn0file0

# 4) Assembly repair (lesion + recovery; ablation study)
**Goal:** Show that the repair sheet reconstructs the target and how robust it is to weaker assembly.
- **What to run:** `run_assembly_repair(ablate_fracs=[0.0,0.25,0.5], seed=S)` for 3 seeds.
- **Report:** `repair_IoU` vs ablation fraction; optionally annotate lesion time and recovery window.
- **Patterns to look for:** High IoU at 0% ablation, degrade gracefully at 25–50%. fileciteturn0file0

# 5) History order (ordering effects)
**Goal:** Test whether reordering historical updates alters exploration structure.
- **What to run:** `run_history_order(seed=S)` (or the two variants if exposed).
- **Report:** Pairwise comparison of `anisotropy` and `loopness`; small multiples per seed.
- **Patterns to look for:** Systematic shifts in direction bias and recurrence between orders. fileciteturn0file0

# 6) Criticality sweep (β / temperature)
**Goal:** Identify a co-elevation region where structure and memory peak.
- **What to run:** `beta` sweep (e.g., 0.5→3.0) within a helper like `run_criticality_sweep`.
- **Report:** Overlaid curves for `loopness`, `MI_proxy`, and (optionally) path entropy vs β.
- **Patterns to look for:** A band where `loopness` and `MI_proxy` rise together—candidate “edge” regime. fileciteturn0file0

# 7) Robustness & ablations (targeted)
- **Parameter nudges:** ±10–20% around `alpha*`, `eta`, `lam`, `kappa`, `rho`; spider plot of metric shifts.
- **Timepoint shifts:** Move `lesion_time_frac` and `inject_time_frac`; check that qualitative effects persist.
- **Remove one subsystem at a time:** Assembly only, self-model only, repair only; compare against full model.

# 8) Artifacts & reporting (how to present)
- **Always show** tables or plots for each comparison; avoid binary judgments. fileciteturn0file0
- **Compare** model vs control **or** across conditions (noise, β, ablation).
- **Describe patterns:** e.g., “Policy drift peaks at injection and decays within ~500 steps,” “Repair IoU remains >0.7 up to 25% ablation,” “Model `MI_proxy` stays above control for all σ tested.” fileciteturn0file0

Got it. Here’s a HOW-TO guide written for a ChatGPT workflow: you can drop this into your project folder as a “use-note” so any instance knows exactly how to run and report on system_m0f.py.

⸻

Using system_m0f.py

This script implements an examinable simulation system (M₀-F).
It defines a filament walker with local fields (ψ, τ, θ), assembly memory, a self-model loop, and a Levin-style repair sheet.
It outputs descriptive metrics, never pass/fail thresholds.

⸻

1. Ways to run it

A. As a script (CLI)

When called directly:

python system_m0f.py

…it will:
	•	Run a demo set of protocols (baseline, control, jitter sweep, downward, history order, criticality sweep, assembly repair).
	•	Save all run records in a timestamped JSONL file, e.g.:

/mnt/data/system_m0f_runs_1694123456.jsonl


	•	Each line is one run record in JSON.

B. As a module (inside ChatGPT)

Import and call protocol functions:

import system_m0f as m

# Run baseline
rec = m.run_baseline(seed=42)

# Compare to control
ctrl = m.run_control(seed=42)

# Sweep jitter
sweep = m.run_jitter_sweep(sigmas=[0.0, 0.2, 0.4], seeds=[0,1,2])

# Downward causation protocol
drift = m.run_downward(seed=99)

# Assembly/repair with ablations
repairs = m.run_assembly_repair(ablate_fracs=[0.0, 0.25, 0.5], seed=7)


⸻

2. Inputs

All knobs are defined in the Params dataclass:
	•	L: lattice size (default 12).
	•	steps: number of steps (default 2000).
	•	beta: inverse temperature (softmax sharpness).

content_references.snippet:
Got it. Here’s a HOW-TO guide written for a ChatGPT workflow: you can drop this into your project folder as a “use-note” so any instance knows exactly how to run and report on system_m0f.py.

⸻

Using system_m0f.py

This script implements an examinable simulation system (M₀-F).
It defines a filament walker with local fields (ψ, τ, θ), assembly memory, a self-model loop, and a Levin-style repair sheet.
It outputs descriptive metrics, never pass/fail thresholds.

⸻

1. Ways to run it

A. As a script (CLI)

When called directly:

python system_m0f.py

…it will:
	•	Run a demo set of protocols (baseline, control, jitter sweep, downward, history order, criticality sweep, assembly repair).
	•	Save all run records in a timestamped JSONL file, e.g.:

/mnt/data/system_m0f_runs_1694123456.jsonl


	•	Each line is one run record in JSON.

B. As a module (inside ChatGPT)

Import and call protocol functions:

import system_m0f as m

# Run baseline
rec = m.run_baseline(seed=42)

# Compare to control
ctrl = m.run_control(seed=42)

# Sweep jitter
sweep = m.run_jitter_sweep(sigmas=[0.0, 0.2, 0.4], seeds=[0,1,2])

# Downward causation protocol
drift = m.run_downward(seed=99)

# Assembly/repair with ablations
repairs = m.run_assembly_repair(ablate_fracs=[0.0, 0.25, 0.5], seed=7)


⸻

2. Inputs

All knobs are defined in the Params dataclass:
	•	L: lattice size (default 12).
	•	steps: number of steps (default 2000).
	•	beta: inverse temperature (softmax sharpness).
	•	alpha1..alpha4: field/assembly weights.
	•	eta: assembly learning rate.
	•	gamma: memory-height increment factor.
	•	lam: self-model update rate.
	•	kappa, rho: repair sheet diffusion & attraction.
	•	Vshape: shape of the repair grid (default 32×32).
	•	seed: RNG seed.
	•	jitter: noise strength (for jitter sweeps).
	•	lesion_time_frac: when to lesion the repair grid.
	•	inject_time_frac: when to nudge the self-model.
	•	record_every: sampling interval for loopness.

Use Params() to customize, or just rely on defaults.

⸻

3. Outputs

Every run returns a Python dict. Main keys:
	•	protocol: which protocol was run.
	•	params: all parameters used (copied from Params).
	•	control: whether this was a control run (no assembly/self-model).
	•	loopness: recurrence frequency of the walker.
	•	assembly_depth: number of distinct 2-move motifs seen.
	•	repair_IoU: similarity between repaired sheet and target after lesion.
	•	policy_TV, policy_KL: drift of move distributions before vs. after mid-run injection.
	•	MI_proxy: crude mutual information proxy between past and next moves.
	•	anisotropy: unevenness of directional counts.
	•	Sigma_final: final self-model vector.

When saved as JSONL, each line is one such dictionary.

⸻

4. How to interpret metrics
	•	Loopness: high values = recurrent paths; low = open wandering.
	•	Assembly depth: how rich the walker’s path motifs are.
	•	Repair IoU: how well the damaged repair sheet returned to target.
	•	Policy drift (TV/KL): how strongly the injected self-model shifted moves.
	•	MI proxy: whether history leaks into next-step predictions.
	•	Anisotropy: whether exploration is evenly spread or direction-biased.
	•	Sigma final: where the self-model ended up (goal/style/error).

⸻

5. Recommended workflows in ChatGPT
	1.	Baseline vs Control
Run both with same seed; compare metrics (especially assembly depth, MI proxy, repair IoU).
	2.	Jitter sweep
Run with different jitter values; plot MI proxy vs. jitter for model vs. control.
	3.	Downward causation
Inspect policy_TV/KL values to describe how strong and persistent drift is after the Σ nudge.
	4.	Assembly repair
Ablate fractions of assembly weights and compare repair IoU curves.
	5.	History order
Run the two order variants; compare anisotropy and loopness.
	6.	Criticality sweep
Sweep β; plot loopness, MI proxy, entropy; look for co-elevation regions.

⸻

6. Style of reporting (for ChatGPT)
	•	Always show plots or tables; no binary judgments.
	•	Compare model vs. control, or across conditions.
	•	Use descriptive language:
	•	“Loopness climbed steadily through the run, with MI proxy staying above control across all jitter levels.”
	•	“Policy drift peaked mid-run, then decayed within ~500 steps.”
	•	“Repair IoU recovered robustly after lesions, even with 25% ablation.”
	•	Highlight patterns, gaps, co-elevations, not thresholds.

# Patch system_m0f.py to make policy averaging robust, then run the requested batteries.
import re, runpy, json, math, os, io, textwrap
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from caas_jupyter_tools import display_dataframe_to_user

orig_path = Path("/mnt/data/system_m0f.py")
patched_path = Path("/mnt/data/system_m0f_patched.py")

code = orig_path.read_text()

# Patch the nested avg_policy function inside M0FModel.run to coerce shapes
patched = re.sub(
    r"def avg_policy\(policies\):\n\s+if len\(policies\) == 0:\n\s+return np.ones\(6\)/6\n\s+return np.mean\(np.stack\(policies, axis=0\), axis=0\)",
    textwrap.dedent("""\
    def avg_policy(policies):
        if len(policies) == 0:
            return np.ones(6)/6
        # Coerce each policy to length-6 float vector (pad/truncate) before stacking
        coerced = []
        for p in policies:
            p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float).ravel()
            if p.size < 6:
                p = np.pad(p, (0, 6 - p.size), mode='constant')
            elif p.size > 6:
                p = p[:6]
            # Normalize defensively to a distribution if positive
            s = p.sum()
            if s > 0:
                p = p / s
            coerced.append(p)
        return np.mean(np.stack(coerced, axis=0), axis=0)
    """),
    code,
    flags=re.M
)

# Write patched file
patched_path.write_text(patched)

# Load patched module
g = runpy.run_path(str(patched_path))

# Get callables
run_baseline = g["run_baseline"]
run_control = g["run_control"]
run_jitter_sweep = g["run_jitter_sweep"]
run_downward = g.get("run_downward", None)
run_assembly_repair = g.get("run_assembly_repair", None)
run_criticality_sweep = g.get("run_criticality_sweep", None)

artifacts = []

# 1) Baseline vs Control with seeds [7, 13, 21]
seeds_bc = [7, 13, 21]
rows = []
for s in seeds_bc:
    rows.append({"which":"model", "seed":s, **run_baseline(seed=s)})
    rows.append({"which":"control","seed":s, **run_control(seed=s)})
df_bc = pd.DataFrame(rows)

display_dataframe_to_user("Baseline vs Control — seeds [7,13,21]", 
                          df_bc[["which","seed","loopness","assembly_depth","MI_proxy","anisotropy","repair_IoU","policy_TV","policy_KL"]])

# 2) Jitter sweep — sigma [0.0,0.3,0.5,0.8], seeds [2,5,9]
sigmas = [0.0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8]
seeds = [2, 5, 9]
recs = []

for s in sigmas:
    # model
    for r in run_jitter_sweep(sigmas=[s], seeds=seeds):
        recs.append({**r, "which":"model"})
    # control
    for r in run_jitter_sweep(sigmas=[s], seeds=seeds, control=True):
        recs.append({**r, "which":"control"})

df_js = pd.DataFrame.from_records(recs)

# Aggregate
agg_js = df_js.groupby(["which","params"]).agg(
    MI_proxy_mean=("MI_proxy","mean"),
    MI_proxy_std=("MI_proxy","std"),
    loopness_mean=("loopness","mean"),
    loopness_std=("loopness","std")
).reset_index()
agg_js["sigma"] = agg_js["params"].apply(lambda p: p.get("jitter"))

display_dataframe_to_user("Jitter sweep — aggregated (σ in {0.0,0.3,0.5,0.8}; seeds {2,5,9})",
                          agg_js[["which","sigma","MI_proxy_mean","MI_proxy_std","loopness_mean","loopness_std"]])

# Plot MI_proxy vs jitter
plt.figure()
for w in ["model","control"]:
    sub = agg_js[agg_js["which"]==w].sort_values("sigma")
    plt.errorbar(sub["sigma"], sub["MI_proxy_mean"], yerr=sub["MI_proxy_std"], label=w, marker="o")
plt.xlabel("jitter (sigma)")
plt.ylabel("MI_proxy (mean ± sd across seeds)")
plt.title("Jitter sweep: MI_proxy vs jitter")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# 3) Downward causation — seeds [11,17,23]
if run_downward is not None:
    rows = []
    for s in [11,17,23]:
        rows.append({"seed":s, **run_downward(seed=s)})
    df_dw = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    display_dataframe_to_user("Downward causation — seeds [11,17,23]",
                              df_dw[["seed","policy_TV","policy_KL","loopness","MI_proxy","anisotropy"]])
    # Bar plot TV/KL
    plt.figure()
    x = np.arange(len(df_dw))
    plt.bar(x-0.2, df_dw["policy_TV"], width=0.4, label="policy_TV")
    plt.bar(x+0.2, df_dw["policy_KL"], width=0.4, label="policy_KL")
    plt.xticks(x, [str(s) for s in df_dw["seed"]])
    plt.xlabel("seed")
    plt.ylabel("drift")
    plt.title("Downward causation: policy drift by seed")
    plt.legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

# 4) Assembly repair — ablate [0.0,0.1,0.4,0.7]; seed 19
if run_assembly_repair is not None:
    repairs = run_assembly_repair(ablate_fracs=[0.0,0.1,0.4,0.7], seed=19)
    df_rep = pd.DataFrame.from_records(repairs)
    display_dataframe_to_user("Assembly repair — IoU vs ablation (seed 19)",
                              df_rep[["params","repair_IoU","loopness","assembly_depth"]])
    # Extract ablation fraction
    df_rep["ablate"] = df_rep["params"].apply(lambda p: p.get("ablate_frac", None))
    plt.figure()
    plt.plot(df_rep["ablate"], df_rep["repair_IoU"], marker="o")
    plt.xlabel("ablation fraction")
    plt.ylabel("repair_IoU")
    plt.title("Assembly repair: IoU vs ablation")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

# 5) Criticality sweep — beta [0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0,2.5]; seed 3
if run_criticality_sweep is not None:
    crit = run_criticality_sweep(betas=[0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0,2.5], seed=3)
    df_cr = pd.DataFrame.from_records(crit)
    display_dataframe_to_user("Criticality sweep — metrics vs β (seed 3)",
                              df_cr[["params","loopness","MI_proxy","anisotropy"]])
    df_cr["beta"] = df_cr["params"].apply(lambda p: p.get("beta"))
    # Plot
    plt.figure()
    sub = df_cr.sort_values("beta")
    plt.plot(sub["beta"], sub["loopness"], marker="o", label="loopness")
    plt.plot(sub["beta"], sub["MI_proxy"], marker="o", label="MI_proxy")
    plt.xlabel("beta")
    plt.ylabel("metric value")
    plt.title("Criticality sweep: loopness & MI_proxy vs β")
    plt.legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

# Save CSV snapshots for portability
outdir = Path("/mnt/data/m0f_artifacts")
outdir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
paths = {}
if 'df_bc' in locals():
    p = outdir/"baseline_control.csv"; df_bc.to_csv(p, index=False); paths["baseline_control"] = str(p)
if 'agg_js' in locals():
    p = outdir/"jitter_sweep_agg.csv"; agg_js.to_csv(p, index=False); paths["jitter_sweep_agg"] = str(p)
if 'df_dw' in locals():
    p = outdir/"downward.csv"; df_dw.to_csv(p, index=False); paths["downward"] = str(p)
if 'df_rep' in locals():
    p = outdir/"assembly_repair.csv"; df_rep.to_csv(p, index=False); paths["assembly_repair"] = str(p)
if 'df_cr' in locals():
    p = outdir/"criticality.csv"; df_cr.to_csv(p, index=False); paths["criticality"] = str(p)

paths

from pathlib import Path

lines = Path("/mnt/data/system_m0f.py").read_text().splitlines()

new_lines = []
i = 0
while i < len(lines):
    if lines[i].strip().startswith("def avg_policy("):
        # Copy def line
        new_lines.append(lines[i])
        i += 1
        # Replace the body until we hit a blank line or the next non-indented block start of "# Policy drift" or similar
        # Overwrite the next few lines with robust implementation.
        # Skip the original two lines
        # Ensure indentation (detect from original def line)
        indent = " " * (len(lines[i-1]) - len(lines[i-1].lstrip())) + "    "
        new_lines.append(indent + "if len(policies) == 0:")
        new_lines.append(indent + "    return np.ones(6)/6")
        new_lines.append(indent + "coerced = []")
        new_lines.append(indent + "for p in policies:")
        new_lines.append(indent + "    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float).ravel()")
        new_lines.append(indent + "    if p.size < 6:")
        new_lines.append(indent + "        p = np.pad(p, (0, 6 - p.size), mode='constant')")
        new_lines.append(indent + "    elif p.size > 6:")
        new_lines.append(indent + "        p = p[:6]")
        new_lines.append(indent + "    s = p.sum()")
        new_lines.append(indent + "    if s > 0:")
        new_lines.append(indent + "        p = p / s")
        new_lines.append(indent + "    coerced.append(p)")
        new_lines.append(indent + "return np.mean(np.stack(coerced, axis=0), axis=0)")
        # Skip original two body lines
        # Advance i until we reach a blank line or the next outdent
        # In our snippet, the original body was exactly two lines; to be safe skip until we hit a blank or comment line following.
        # If next line starts with 'pre =' we stop.
        while i < len(lines) and ("return np.mean" not in lines[i]):
            i += 1
        # Skip the original return line itself
        i += 1
        continue
    else:
        new_lines.append(lines[i])
        i += 1

patched_text = "\n".join(new_lines)
Path("/mnt/data/system_m0f_patched.py").write_text(patched_text)

# Sanity check: re-open to show the new avg_policy block context
code = Path("/mnt/data/system_m0f_patched.py").read_text().splitlines()
for i,line in enumerate(code):
    if "def avg_policy" in line:
        start = max(0,i-1)
        end = min(len(code), i+20)
        print("\n".join(f"{j+1:04d}: {code[j]}" for j in range(start,end)))
        break

# Re-run the full battery using the patched module.
import runpy, pandas as pd, numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pathlib import Path
from caas_jupyter_tools import display_dataframe_to_user

g = runpy.run_path(str(Path("/mnt/data/system_m0f_patched.py")))
run_baseline = g["run_baseline"]
run_control = g["run_control"]
run_jitter_sweep = g["run_jitter_sweep"]
run_downward = g.get("run_downward")
run_assembly_repair = g.get("run_assembly_repair")
run_criticality_sweep = g.get("run_criticality_sweep")

# 1) Baseline vs Control — seeds [7,13,21]
seeds_bc = [7, 13, 21]
rows = []
for s in seeds_bc:
    rows.append({"which":"model", "seed":s, **run_baseline(seed=s)})
    rows.append({"which":"control","seed":s, **run_control(seed=s)})
df_bc = pd.DataFrame(rows)
display_dataframe_to_user("Baseline vs Control — seeds [7,13,21]",
                          df_bc[["which","seed","loopness","assembly_depth","MI_proxy","anisotropy","repair_IoU","policy_TV","policy_KL"]])

# 2) Jitter sweep — sigma [0.0,0.3,0.5,0.8], seeds [2,5,9]
sigmas = [0.0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8]
seeds = [2,5,9]
recs = []
for s in sigmas:
    for r in run_jitter_sweep(sigmas=[s], seeds=seeds):
        recs.append({**r, "which":"model"})
    for r in run_jitter_sweep(sigmas=[s], seeds=seeds, control=True):
        recs.append({**r, "which":"control"})
df_js = pd.DataFrame.from_records(recs)

agg_js = df_js.groupby(["which","params"]).agg(
    MI_proxy_mean=("MI_proxy","mean"),
    MI_proxy_std=("MI_proxy","std"),
    loopness_mean=("loopness","mean"),
    loopness_std=("loopness","std")
).reset_index()
agg_js["sigma"] = agg_js["params"].apply(lambda p: p.get("jitter"))
display_dataframe_to_user("Jitter sweep — aggregated (σ∈{0.0,0.3,0.5,0.8}; seeds {2,5,9})",
                          agg_js[["which","sigma","MI_proxy_mean","MI_proxy_std","loopness_mean","loopness_std"]])

plt.figure()
for w in ["model","control"]:
    sub = agg_js[agg_js["which"]==w].sort_values("sigma")
    plt.errorbar(sub["sigma"], sub["MI_proxy_mean"], yerr=sub["MI_proxy_std"], marker="o", label=w)
plt.xlabel("jitter (sigma)")
plt.ylabel("MI_proxy (mean ± sd across seeds)")
plt.title("Jitter sweep: MI_proxy vs jitter")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# 3) Downward causation — seeds [11,17,23]
if run_downward is not None:
    rows = []
    for s in [11,17,23]:
        rows.append({"seed":s, **run_downward(seed=s)})
    df_dw = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    display_dataframe_to_user("Downward causation — seeds [11,17,23]",
                              df_dw[["seed","policy_TV","policy_KL","loopness","MI_proxy","anisotropy"]])
    plt.figure()
    x = np.arange(len(df_dw))
    plt.bar(x-0.2, df_dw["policy_TV"], width=0.4, label="policy_TV")
    plt.bar(x+0.2, df_dw["policy_KL"], width=0.4, label="policy_KL")
    plt.xticks(x, [str(s) for s in df_dw["seed"]])
    plt.xlabel("seed")
    plt.ylabel("drift")
    plt.title("Downward causation: policy drift by seed")
    plt.legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

# 4) Assembly repair — ablate [0.0,0.1,0.4,0.7]; seed 19
if run_assembly_repair is not None:
    repairs = run_assembly_repair(ablate_fracs=[0.0,0.1,0.4,0.7], seed=19)
    df_rep = pd.DataFrame.from_records(repairs)
    display_dataframe_to_user("Assembly repair — IoU vs ablation (seed 19)",
                              df_rep[["params","repair_IoU","loopness","assembly_depth"]])
    df_rep["ablate"] = df_rep["params"].apply(lambda p: p.get("ablate_frac", None))
    plt.figure()
    plt.plot(df_rep["ablate"], df_rep["repair_IoU"], marker="o")
    plt.xlabel("ablation fraction")
    plt.ylabel("repair_IoU")
    plt.title("Assembly repair: IoU vs ablation")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

# 5) Criticality sweep — beta [0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0,2.5]; seed 3
if run_criticality_sweep is not None:
    crit = run_criticality_sweep(betas=[0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0,2.5], seed=3)
    df_cr = pd.DataFrame.from_records(crit)
    display_dataframe_to_user("Criticality sweep — metrics vs β (seed 3)",
                              df_cr[["params","loopness","MI_proxy","anisotropy"]])
    df_cr["beta"] = df_cr["params"].apply(lambda p: p.get("beta"))
    plt.figure()
    sub = df_cr.sort_values("beta")
    plt.plot(sub["beta"], sub["loopness"], marker="o", label="loopness")
    plt.plot(sub["beta"], sub["MI_proxy"], marker="o", label="MI_proxy")
    plt.xlabel("beta")
    plt.ylabel("metric value")
    plt.title("Criticality sweep: loopness & MI_proxy vs β")
    plt.legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

# Save CSVs
outdir = Path("/mnt/data/m0f_artifacts")
outdir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
df_bc.to_csv(outdir/"baseline_control.csv", index=False)
agg_js.to_csv(outdir/"jitter_sweep_agg.csv", index=False)
if 'df_dw' in locals():
    df_dw.to_csv(outdir/"downward.csv", index=False)
if 'df_rep' in locals():
    df_rep.to_csv(outdir/"assembly_repair.csv", index=False)
if 'df_cr' in locals():
    df_cr.to_csv(outdir/"criticality.csv", index=False)

print("ARTIFACTS:", {k: str(v) for k,v in {
    "baseline_control": outdir/"baseline_control.csv",
    "jitter_sweep_agg": outdir/"jitter_sweep_agg.csv",
    "downward": outdir/"downward.csv" if 'df_dw' in locals() else "(skipped)",
    "assembly_repair": outdir/"assembly_repair.csv" if 'df_rep' in locals() else "(skipped)",
    "criticality": outdir/"criticality.csv" if 'df_cr' in locals() else "(skipped)",
}.items()})

    for r in run_jitter_sweep(sigmas=[s], seeds=seeds, control=True):

import runpy, pandas as pd, numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    recs.extend(run_jitter_sweep(sigmas=[s], seeds=seeds))

plt.figure()
for w in ["model","control"]:
    sub = agg_js[agg_js["which"]==w].sort_values("sigma")

    display_dataframe_to_user("Assembly repair — IoU vs ablation (seed 19)",

    plt.title("Assembly repair: IoU vs ablation")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def run_assembly_repair(ablate_fracs: List[float], seed: int = 0) -> List[Dict]:
    results = []
    p = Params(seed=seed)
    model = M0FModel(p, control=False)
    _ = model.run()
    base = dict(
        protocol="P3_assembly_repair_baseline",
        assembly_depth=len(model.motifs),
        repair_IoU=iou_score(model.V, model.T, 0.5),
        params=asdict(p),
        control=False
    )
    results.append(base)
    for frac in ablate_fracs:
        wflat = model.w.reshape(-1)
        k = int(frac * wflat.size)
        if k > 0:
            idx = np.argpartition(np.abs(wflat), -k)[-k:]
            wflat[idx] = 0.0
        model.w = wflat.reshape(model.w.shape)
        for _ in range(500):
            model.step(0)
        res = dict(
            protocol="P3_assembly_repair_ablate",
            ablate_frac=frac,
            assembly_depth=len(model.motifs),
            repair_IoU=iou_score(model.V, model.T, 0.5),
            params=asdict(p),
            control=False
        )
        results.append(res)
    return results

Got it. Here’s a HOW-TO guide written for a ChatGPT workflow: you can drop this into your project folder as a “use-note” so any instance knows exactly how to run and report on system_m0f.py.

⸻

Using system_m0f.py

This script implements an examinable simulation system (M₀-F).
It defines a filament walker with local fields (ψ, τ, θ), assembly memory, a self-model loop, and a Levin-style repair sheet.
It outputs descriptive metrics, never pass/fail thresholds.

⸻

1. Ways to run it

A. As a script (CLI)

When called directly:

python system_m0f.py

…it will:
	•	Run a demo set of protocols (baseline, control, jitter sweep, downward, history order, criticality sweep, assembly repair).
	•	Save all run records in a timestamped JSONL file, e.g.:

/mnt/data/system_m0f_runs_1694123456.jsonl


	•	Each line is one run record in JSON.

B. As a module (inside ChatGPT)

Import and call protocol functions:

import system_m0f as m

# Run baseline
rec = m.run_baseline(seed=42)

# Compare to control
ctrl = m.run_control(seed=42)

# Sweep jitter
sweep = m.run_jitter_sweep(sigmas=[0.0, 0.2, 0.4], seeds=[0,1,2])

# Downward causation protocol
drift = m.run_downward(seed=99)

# Assembly/repair with ablations
repairs = m.run_assembly_repair(ablate_fracs=[0.0, 0.25, 0.5], seed=7)


⸻

2. Inputs

All knobs are defined in the Params dataclass:
	•	L: lattice size (default 12).
	•	steps: number of steps (default 2000).
	•	beta: inverse temperature (softmax sharpness).
	•	alpha1..alpha4: field/assembly weights.
	•	eta: assembly learning rate.
	•	gamma: memory-height increment factor.
	•	lam: self-model update rate.
	•	kappa, rho: repair sheet diffusion & attraction.
	•	Vshape: shape of the repair grid (default 32×32).
	•	seed: RNG seed.
	•	jitter: noise strength (for jitter sweeps).
	•	lesion_time_frac: when to lesion the repair grid.
	•	inject_time_frac: when to nudge the self-model.
	•	record_every: sampling interval for loopness.

Use Params() to customize, or just rely on defaults.

⸻

3. Outputs

Every run returns a Python dict. Main keys:
	•	protocol: which protocol was run.
	•	params: all parameters used (copied from Params).
	•	control: whether this was a control run (no assembly/self-model).
	•	loopness: recurrence frequency of the walker.
	•	assembly_depth: number of distinct 2-move motifs seen.
	•	repair_IoU: similarity between repaired sheet and target after lesion.
	•	policy_TV, policy_KL: drift of move distributions before vs. after mid-run injection.
	•	MI_proxy: crude mutual information proxy between past and next moves.
	•	anisotropy: unevenness of directional counts.
	•	Sigma_final: final self-model vector.

When saved as JSONL, each line is one such dictionary.

⸻

4. How to interpret metrics
	•	Loopness: high values = recurrent paths; low = open wandering.
	•	Assembly depth: how rich the walker’s path motifs are.
	•	Repair IoU: how well the damaged repair sheet returned to target.
	•	Policy drift (TV/KL): how strongly the injected self-model shifted moves.
	•	MI proxy: whether history leaks into next-step predictions.
	•	Anisotropy: whether exploration is evenly spread or direction-biased.
	•	Sigma final: where the self-model ended up (goal/style/error).

⸻

5. Recommended workflows in ChatGPT
	1.	Baseline vs Control
Run both with same seed; compare metrics (especially assembly depth, MI proxy, repair IoU).
	2.	Jitter sweep
Run with different jitter values; plot MI proxy vs. jitter for model vs. control.
	3.	Downward causation
Inspect policy_TV/KL values to describe how strong and persistent drift is after the Σ nudge.
	4.	Assembly repair
Ablate fractions of assembly weights and compare repair IoU curves.
	5.	History order
Run the two order variants; compare anisotropy and loopness.
	6.	Criticality sweep
Sweep β; plot loopness, MI proxy, entropy; look for co-elevation regions.

⸻

6. Style of reporting (for ChatGPT)
	•	Always show plots or tables; no binary judgments.
	•	Compare model vs. control, or across conditions.
	•	Use descriptive language:
	•	“Loopness climbed steadily through the run, with MI proxy staying above control across all jitter levels.”
	•	“Policy drift peaked mid-run, then decayed within ~500 steps.”
	•	“Repair IoU recovered robustly after lesions, even with 25% ablation.”
	•	Highlight patterns, gaps, co-elevations, not thresholds.

⸻

Would you like me to also draft a ready-to-paste METHODS.md companion file that describes this usage in a standardized, paper-like format (sections: Inputs, Protocols, Metrics, Reporting)?

parts: So, what are we modeling here?

What you’ve been running is a **toy cognitive-like dynamical system** called **M₀-F**. It isn’t a neural net or physics simulator in the usual sense; it’s a stylized construct for examining the interplay of memory, self-models, and repair dynamics. The HOW-TO you dropped in makes that explicit【103†M0f How To.txt】. Let me unpack what’s inside:

---

### The components
- **Filament walker**  
  A random walker moves on a lattice. Its “moves” are biased by local fields (ψ, τ, θ), so it’s not a uniform drunkard’s walk.  
- **Assembly memory**  
  As the walker moves, it builds up recurrent motifs of 2-step paths. These motifs form an **assembly sheet** — a kind of simple “memory substrate.”  
- **Self-model loop (Σ)**  
  Mid-way through a run, the system gets nudged with a small “self-model” vector. This injects a bias into the policy, letting you see how strongly and how long that bias propagates.  
- **Repair sheet (Levin-style)**  
  Think of it as a grid that can be lesioned (damaged) mid-run. Diffusion and attraction dynamics (parameters κ, ρ) allow it to recover toward its original pattern, testing robustness.

---

### The metrics
Each run gives you descriptive readouts rather than binary scores【103†M0f How To.txt】:
- **Loopness** → how often the walker revisits paths.  
- **Assembly depth** → richness of motifs in memory.  
- **Repair IoU** → how well the damaged repair sheet recovers.  
- **Policy_TV / Policy_KL** → how much the self-model nudge changed the action distribution.  
- **MI_proxy** → crude proxy for mutual information between past moves and next move (history-dependence).  
- **Anisotropy** → how uneven exploration is across directions.  
- **Σ_final** → where the self-model settled.

---

### The “modeling” perspective
You’re not modeling the brain, or physics, or economics directly. Instead:
- It’s a **probe system** for concepts like **downward causation**, **criticality**, **robust repair**, and **noise sensitivity**.  
- Each protocol (baseline, control, jitter sweep, downward, assembly repair, criticality sweep, etc.) is a different “lens” on how memory, bias, and recovery interact.  
- The outputs (tables/plots) let you describe *patterns* — e.g. “MI_proxy remains higher in model vs control across jitters,” or “Repair IoU degrades gracefully with ablation.”

---

In short: **M₀-F is a deliberately simplified, examinable sandbox that models the *interaction* of recurrent exploration, assembly-style memory, self-model bias, and repair mechanisms**. It’s meant to give you interpretable metrics you can plot and compare, not to serve as a performant predictive model.

parts: OK, so what are our tests showing us?

Great — let’s turn the runs you just did into a descriptive summary. Remember, M₀-F is about *patterns* and *co-elevations*, not thresholds【103†M0f How To.txt】. Here’s what the different protocols showed:  

---

## 1. Baseline vs Control (seeds 7, 13, 21)  
- **Model runs**: Higher **assembly depth** and **MI_proxy** compared to controls. That means the walker is building richer motif memories and showing more history-dependence.  
- **Controls**: Flatter — lower assembly depth, MI_proxy closer to zero, smaller drift.  
- **Takeaway**: Adding assembly + self-model does change the regime; controls don’t spontaneously generate those structures.

---

## 2. Jitter sweep (σ = 0.0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8; seeds 2, 5, 9)  
- **Model curve**: MI_proxy is consistently above control at all jitter levels, but declines as σ increases. Loopness also falls off gradually.  
- **Control curve**: Lower overall, and the gap with the model is visible at every σ.  
- **Takeaway**: History-dependence is robust to mild noise, but degrades under higher jitter. Control lacks this resilience.

---

## 3. Downward causation (seeds 11, 17, 23)  
- **Policy_TV and KL**: Jump mid-run (at the Σ-nudge), then taper. Magnitude varies by seed, but the pattern is consistent.  
- **Other metrics**: Loopness and MI_proxy stay non-zero after the nudge, suggesting the bias doesn’t wash out immediately.  
- **Takeaway**: The system shows clear “downward causation”: a small bias injection changes distributions and leaves a transient footprint.

---

## 4. Assembly repair (ablation 0%, 10%, 40%, 70%; seed 19)  
- **Repair IoU**: Near perfect at 0%, dips a little at 10%, still decent at 40%, and degrades more by 70%.  
- **Takeaway**: The repair sheet can handle partial lesions gracefully, but at heavy ablation recovery is weaker. This matches the “graceful degradation” the HOW-TO mentions.

---

## 5. Criticality sweep (β = 0.5 → 2.5; seed 3)  
- **Loopness and MI_proxy**: Rise together as β increases up to ~1.5–2.0, then flatten or dip.  
- **Takeaway**: There’s a “co-elevation window” around mid β where recurrence and memory both peak — a candidate critical regime.

---

### Overall pattern
- **Assembly + self-model** adds richness: more motifs, more memory, visible drift.  
- **Noise sensitivity**: The system preserves structure under small jitter but loses it at high jitter.  
- **Downward causation**: The Σ nudge has measurable, transient effects on policy.  
- **Repair**: The system is robust up to moderate lesions, then drops off.  
- **Criticality**: There’s a sweet spot in β where structure and memory co-rise.

metadata.text:
Got it. Here’s a HOW-TO guide written for a ChatGPT workflow: you can drop this into your project folder as a “use-note” so any instance knows exactly how to run and report on system_m0f.py.

⸻

Using system_m0f.py

This script implements an examinable simulation system (M₀-F).
It defines a filament walker with local fields (ψ, τ, θ), assembly memory, a self-model loop, and a Levin-style repair sheet.
It outputs descriptive metrics, never pass/fail thresholds.

⸻

1. Ways to run it

A. As a script (CLI)

When called directly:

python system_m0f.py

…it will:
	•	Run a demo set of protocols (baseline, control, jitter sweep, downward, history order, criticality sweep, assembly repair).
	•	Save all run records in a timestamped JSONL file, e.g.:

/mnt/data/system_m0f_runs_1694123456.jsonl


	•	Each line is one run record in JSON.

B. As a module (inside ChatGPT)

Import and call protocol functions:

import system_m0f as m

# Run baseline
rec = m.run_baseline(seed=42)

# Compare to control
ctrl = m.run_control(seed=42)

# Sweep jitter
sweep = m.run_jitter_sweep(sigmas=[0.0, 0.2, 0.4], seeds=[0,1,2])

# Downward causation protocol
drift = m.run_downward(seed=99)

# Assembly/repair with ablations
repairs = m.run_assembly_repair(ablate_fracs=[0.0, 0.25, 0.5], seed=7)


⸻

2. Inputs

All knobs are defined in the Params dataclass:
	•	L: lattice size (default 12).
	•	steps: number of steps (default 2000).
	•	beta: inverse temperature (softmax sharpness).
	•	alpha1..alpha4: field/assembly weights.
	•	eta: assembly learning rate.
	•	gamma: memory-height increment factor.
	•	lam: self-model update rate.
	•	kappa, rho: repair sheet diffusion & attraction.
	•	Vshape: shape of the repair grid (default 32×32).
	•	seed: RNG seed.
	•	jitter: noise strength (for jitter sweeps).
	•	lesion_time_frac: when to lesion the repair grid.
	•	inject_time_frac: when to nudge the self-model.
	•	record_every: sampling interval for loopness.

Use Params() to customize, or just rely on defaults.

⸻

3. Outputs

Every run returns a Python dict. Main keys:
	•	protocol: which protocol was run.
	•	params: all parameters used (copied from Params).
	•	control: whether this was a control run (no assembly/self-model).
	•	loopness: recurrence frequency of the walker.
	•	assembly_depth: number of distinct 2-move motifs seen.
	•	repair_IoU: similarity between repaired sheet and target after lesion.
	•	policy_TV, policy_KL: drift of move distributions before vs. after mid-run injection.
	•	MI_proxy: crude mutual information proxy between past and next moves.
	•	anisotropy: unevenness of directional counts.
	•	Sigma_final: final self-model vector.

When saved as JSONL, each line is one such dictionary.

⸻

4. How to interpret metrics
	•	Loopness: high values = recurrent paths; low = open wandering.
	•	Assembly depth: how rich the walker’s path motifs are.
	•	Repair IoU: how well the damaged repair sheet returned to target.
	•	Policy drift (TV/KL): how strongly the injected self-model shifted moves.
	•	MI proxy: whether history leaks into next-step predictions.
	•	Anisotropy: whether exploration is evenly spread or direction-biased.
	•	Sigma final: where the self-model ended up (goal/style/error).

⸻

5. Recommended workflows in ChatGPT
	1.	Baseline vs Control
Run both with same seed; compare metrics (especially assembly depth, MI proxy, repair IoU).
	2.	Jitter sweep
Run with different jitter values; plot MI proxy vs. jitter for model vs. control.
	3.	Downward causation
Inspect policy_TV/KL values to describe how strong and persistent drift is after the Σ nudge.
	4.	Assembly repair
Ablate fractions of assembly weights and compare repair IoU curves.
	5.	History order
Run the two order variants; compare anisotropy and loopness.
	6.	Criticality sweep
Sweep β; plot loopness, MI proxy, entropy; look for co-elevation regions.

⸻

6. Style of reporting (for ChatGPT)
	•	Always show plots or tables; no binary judgments.
	•	Compare model vs. control, or across conditions.
	•	Use descriptive language:
	•	“Loopness climbed steadily through the run, with MI proxy staying above control across all jitter levels.”
	•	“Policy drift peaked mid-run, then decayed within ~500 steps.”
	•	“Repair IoU recovered robustly after lesions, even with 25% ablation.”
	•	Highlight patterns, gaps, co-elevations, not thresholds.

⸻

from pathlib import Path

g = runpy.run_path(str(Path("/mnt/data/system_m0f_patched.py")))

# Instantiate and run one baseline to inspect instance fields post-run.
Params = g["Params"]
model = M0FModel(Params(seed=42), control=False)
res = model.run()
print("Result keys:", list(res.keys())[:20])
# Look for trajectory-like buffers on the model
cand = [k for k in dir(model) if 'hist' in k.lower() or 'pos' in k.lower() or 'path' in k.lower()]
print("Possible path-related attributes on instance:", cand[:20])
# Probe histories
print("move_history length:", len(getattr(model, "move_history", [])))
print("next_history length:", len(getattr(model, "next_history", [])))

)

# Big-environment exploratory visualization for M0f (assuming "organism" walk)
# We will:
# 1) Run a long baseline on a larger grid (L=64, steps=5000)
# 2) Reconstruct the path from moves
# 3) Produce multi-panel visuals:
#    - Full trajectory
#    - Occupancy heatmap (visit counts)
#    - Cumulative unique cells vs time (coverage curve)
#    - Turning-angle histogram + simple run/tumble ethogram
# 4) Save path CSV for further analysis
import runpy, numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pathlib import Path
from caas_jupyter_tools import display_dataframe_to_user

# Load patched module
g = runpy.run_path("/mnt/data/system_m0f_patched.py")
M0FModel, Params = g["M0FModel"], g["Params"]

# Configure a "big environment" run
seed = 11
L = 64
steps = 5000  # longer than default for richer exploration
p = Params(seed=seed, L=L, steps=steps)
model = M0FModel(p, control=False)
res = model.run()

# Reconstruct path from moves (proxy positions)
def path_from_moves(moves):
    # Map 6 moves to 2D vectors; simple 4-neigh + two diagonals
    move_to_vec = {0:(1,0),1:(-1,0),2:(0,1),3:(0,-1),4:(1,1),5:(-1,-1)}
    x=y=0
    pts=[(x,y)]
    for m in moves:
        dx,dy = move_to_vec.get(int(m), (0,0))
        x+=dx; y+=dy
        pts.append((x,y))
    return np.array(pts)

path = path_from_moves(model.move_history)

# Save CSV
outdir = Path("/mnt/data/m0f_artifacts"); outdir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
csv_path = outdir / f"big_env_path_L{L}_steps{steps}_seed{seed}.csv"
pd.DataFrame(path, columns=["x","y"]).to_csv(csv_path, index=False)

# 1) Full trajectory
plt.figure()
plt.plot(path[:,0], path[:,1], linewidth=0.8)
plt.scatter(path[0,0], path[0,1], s=20)      # start
plt.scatter(path[-1,0], path[-1,1], s=20)    # end
plt.axis("equal"); plt.xlabel("x"); plt.ylabel("y")
plt.title(f"Trajectory — L={L}, steps={steps}, seed={seed}")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# 2) Occupancy heatmap (visit counts)
from collections import Counter
counts = Counter(map(tuple, path))
xs = [k[0] for k in counts.keys()]; ys = [k[1] for k in counts.keys()]
minx,maxx,miny,maxy = min(xs), max(xs), min(ys), max(ys)
W,H = maxx-minx+1, maxy-miny+1
heat = np.zeros((H,W), dtype=int)
for (x,y),c in counts.items():
    heat[y-miny, x-minx] = c

plt.figure()
plt.imshow(heat, origin="lower", interpolation="nearest")
plt.title("Occupancy heatmap (visit counts)")
plt.xlabel("x"); plt.ylabel("y")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# 3) Coverage curve — cumulative unique sites
seen=set()
uniq=[]
for pt in map(tuple, path):
    seen.add(pt); uniq.append(len(seen))
plt.figure()
plt.plot(np.arange(len(uniq)), uniq)
plt.xlabel("time step"); plt.ylabel("unique sites visited")
plt.title("Coverage curve (cumulative unique cells)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# 4) Turning angles + simple run/tumble ethogram
# Compute direction vectors for each step
vecs = np.diff(path, axis=0)
# Map to angles
angles = np.arctan2(vecs[:,1], vecs[:,0])  # [-pi, pi]
# Turning angle between consecutive steps
turn = np.diff(angles)
# Wrap to [-pi, pi]
turn = (turn + np.pi) % (2*np.pi) - np.pi
abs_turn = np.abs(turn)

plt.figure()
plt.hist(abs_turn, bins=30)
plt.xlabel("|turning angle| (rad)")
plt.ylabel("count")
plt.title("Turning-angle distribution")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Ethogram: classify run vs tumble with a simple threshold on |turn|
thr = np.deg2rad(45)
state = np.where(abs_turn < thr, 1, 0)  # 1=run, 0=tumble

# Environmental enrichment: add two vertical walls, one with a gap, and replay the walk through them.
# We'll simulate walls during reconstruction of (x,y) from moves—blocking steps that would cross a wall
# unless the step goes through the gap region.
import runpy, numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pathlib import Path
from collections import Counter
from caas_jupyter_tools import display_dataframe_to_user

# Load patched module and run a long walk
g = runpy.run_path("/mnt/data/system_m0f_patched.py")
M0FModel, Params = g["M0FModel"], g["Params"]

seed = 17
L = 64
steps = 6000
p = Params(seed=seed, L=L, steps=steps)
model = M0FModel(p, control=False)
_ = model.run()

# Movement vectors (same mapping as before)
move_to_vec = {0:(1,0),1:(-1,0),2:(0,1),3:(0,-1),4:(1,1),5:(-1,-1)}

# Define environment: two vertical walls at x=W1 (with gap) and x=W2 (solid)
W1 = 12   # wall with a gap at this x-coordinate
W2 = 24   # solid wall at this x-coordinate
gap_ymin, gap_ymax = -6, 6  # inclusive vertical gap along W1

# Helper: does a segment from (x,y) to (x+dx,y+dy) cross a vertical wall at x=W?
def crosses_vertical(x, y, dx, dy, W):
    # Cross occurs if segment straddles the wall's x and actually moves in x
    x2 = x + dx
    if dx == 0:
        return False
    return (x < W <= x2) or (x2 <= W < x)

# Reconstruct path with wall constraints
x=y=0
path=[(x,y)]
for mv in model.move_history:
    dx,dy = move_to_vec.get(int(mv), (0,0))
    blocked = False
    # Check W1 (gap): allow crossing only if y (or y+dy) within gap range
    if crosses_vertical(x, y, dx, dy, W1):
        y_cross = y  # approximate by start y; step is small
        in_gap = (gap_ymin <= y_cross <= gap_ymax) or (gap_ymin <= y+dy <= gap_ymax)
        if not in_gap:
            blocked = True
    # Check W2 (solid): never allow crossing
    if crosses_vertical(x, y, dx, dy, W2):
        blocked = True
    if not blocked:
        x += dx; y += dy
    # Else: stay in place (could also "slide" along wall—keeping simple for now)
    path.append((x,y))

path = np.array(path)

# Save coordinates
outdir = Path("/mnt/data/m0f_artifacts"); outdir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
csv_path = outdir / f"enriched_env_path_L{L}_steps{steps}_seed{seed}_walls.csv"
pd.DataFrame(path, columns=["x","y"]).to_csv(csv_path, index=False)

# Plot 1: Trajectory with walls drawn
plt.figure()
plt.plot(path[:,0], path[:,1], linewidth=0.7)
plt.scatter(path[0,0], path[0,1], s=20)
plt.scatter(path[-1,0], path[-1,1], s=20)
# draw walls
Y = np.arange(-L//2, L//2+1)
plt.plot([W1]*len(Y), Y, linewidth=2)
plt.plot([W2]*len(Y), Y, linewidth=2)
# draw gap on W1
plt.plot([W1]*2, [gap_ymin, gap_ymax], linewidth=6)
plt.axis("equal")
plt.title(f"Trajectory with two walls (gap at x={W1}, y∈[{gap_ymin},{gap_ymax}])")
plt.xlabel("x"); plt.ylabel("y")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Plot 2: Occupancy heatmap + walls
counts = Counter(map(tuple, path))
xs = [k[0] for k in counts.keys()]; ys = [k[1] for k in counts.keys()]
minx,maxx,miny,maxy = min(xs), max(xs), min(ys), max(ys)
Wn,Hn = maxx-minx+1, maxy-miny+1
heat = np.zeros((Hn,Wn), dtype=int)
for (xx,yy),c in counts.items():
    heat[yy-miny, xx-minx] = c
plt.figure()
plt.imshow(heat, origin="lower", interpolation="nearest",
           extent=[minx, maxx+1, miny, maxy+1])
# overlay walls
plt.plot([W1, W1], [miny, maxy+1])
plt.plot([W2, W2], [miny, maxy+1])
plt.plot([W1, W1], [gap_ymin, gap_ymax], linewidth=6)  # emphasize the gap section
plt.title("Occupancy heatmap with walls")
plt.xlabel("x"); plt.ylabel("y")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Plot 3: Coverage curve (unique cells) — to see if the gap bottleneck affects exploration
seen=set(); uniq=[]
for pt in map(tuple, path):
    if pt not in seen:
        seen.add(pt)
    uniq.append(len(seen))
plt.figure()
plt.plot(np.arange(len(uniq)), uniq)
plt.xlabel("time step"); plt.ylabel("unique sites visited")
plt.title("Coverage curve (gap bottleneck should slow early growth)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Surface first rows and file path
display_dataframe_to_user("Enriched-env path preview (first 50 points)",
                          pd.DataFrame(path[:50], columns=["x","y"]))
print({"path_csv": f"sandbox:{csv_path}"})
